docs.title: Meet Ranger
docs.text:
Ranger is being reorganized

The earlier Ranger stack (a chat API with workflows, MCP and RAG, shipped as a Docker stack or an appliance) is being retired. Ranger is now built from the parts below. These docs describe the new layout and grow as each part lands.

Ranger is AI tooling for cyber range training, exercises and simulation. It helps you design an event, build and run it, and learn from it, using local or frontier models. It works on closed and air-gapped ranges.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
An exercise today lives in pieces: a scenario document, a network build, injects in a spreadsheet, activity in logs, and lessons in someone's notes. A good scenario takes an engineer and days of back-and-forth. Once it's written, every tool that builds or runs the event has to be told the same things again.

AI makes this worse when it works from scraps. A model asked cold invents things: a news story that contradicts the ground truth, a simulated bank clerk who doesn't know which bank they work for, an after-action summary that can't tell the plan from what actually happened.

docs.title: The Parts
docs.text:
Part Status What it does Chronicle Draft One record for the whole event. Apps publish what they add and subscribe to what they need. Scenario Builder Experimental A guided workspace, with an AI agent, for writing the scenario: the world and what the event must achieve. Range Automation Next Builds, runs and adapts the range from the Chronicle.

They fit together like this:

  1. Scenario Builder asks the designer the questions that lead to a good scenario and records every answer, along with who gave it and why. Its output is one scenario JSON document.
  2. That document is the first page of a Chronicle, the record of the event. The Chronicle API stores it and carries every change to the apps that subscribe.
  3. Range Automation and other apps (GraySpace, GHOSTS, the Crucible apps) subscribe to the parts they need, build and run the event, and write back what they built, did and saw.
  4. When the event ends, the Chronicle is the event, ready to seed the next one.

docs.title: Works With
docs.text:
Crucible and GHOSTS

Ranger works alongside the SEI's Crucible Framework, a modular system for creating and managing virtual environments for training and exercises (source, docs), and GHOSTS, which simulates the people on the range (source).

docs.title: Principles
docs.text:
• Local models first. Every part is built and tested to work on an open-weight model such as gemma-4-26b served by Ollama. A frontier model is used where one is available.
  • People decide. The AI drafts and proposes. Nothing a person stated changes without their approval, and every change records who made it.
  • The right eyes only. Ground truth stays with exercise control, and visibility travels with the data, for AI models as well as people.

docs.title: Chronicle
docs.text:
Draft

Chronicle has a draft spec and a running API. Nothing in the spec is settled until the architecture team agrees on it; the schema design lists the decisions still open. The concept brief is src/chronicle/chronicle.html; open it in a browser or print it.

Chronicle is one living record of an event, from the first idea to the last lesson. The event can be training, an exercise or a simulation, run at a table or on a live range.

It starts as the scenario: what the world looks like, and what the event must achieve. Around it, apps publish and subscribe. Each one subscribes to the parts it needs and publishes what it built, did and saw. When the event ends, the Chronicle is the event: complete, attributable, and ready to seed the next one.

docs.title: At a Glance
docs.text: What it is One JSON record per event, with a published, versioned schema How apps connect Publish and subscribe around the record. No app calls another. It starts as The scenario: the world, and what the event must achieve It ends as The event itself: built, run and reviewed Models Local or frontier. Works on a closed range.

docs.title: Four Principles
docs.text:
1. One record, many authors. Each app owns its part. It reads the rest, but writes only what it did.
  2. Publish and subscribe. Apps subscribe to the parts they need and publish what they add. A new app is a new subscriber, not a new integration.
  3. Nothing is overwritten. Every change keeps who made it, when and why, so the record is also the event's history.
  4. The right eyes only. Ground truth stays with exercise control. Participants see only what they should, everywhere.

docs.title: The Record
docs.text:
A Chronicle has five parts, filled in the order the event fills them:

Part What it holds Written by World Sides, organizations, networks, devices, services, personas and pools, vulnerabilities, facts Scenario Builder Intent Objectives, teaching points, rules of play, vocabulary, summaries, the planned events Scenario Builder As Built Deployments, what each planned item became, generated personas and content GraySpace, GHOSTS, Pandora As Run Milestones, cyber and influence activity, injects delivered, participant actions, observations GHOSTS, the exercise apps, exercise control Lessons Assessments against the objectives, lessons for the next event After-action review

Apps don't edit the record. They publish entries: each one adds, revises or retracts one item, and records who made the change, when and why. The parts are rebuilt from the entries, so the record is also its own history. A revise names the version it replaces, so two apps can't silently overwrite each other.

Every item is marked participant, excon (exercise control) or designer. An item nobody marked stays with exercise control, so a forgotten marking can't leak the ground truth. An item can also name the personas, pools or organizations that know it: a simulated bank clerk knows their own bank, but not the twist.

docs.title: Built on the Standards
docs.text:
The spec borrows its names from SISO's standards, so a Chronicle can be exchanged with simulations that already use them:

  • Cyber objects and events use the names of the Cyber Data Exchange Model (SISO-STD-025-2023): a host is a Device, an attack is a PhishingAttack. Enumerated values are written as SISO-REF-010 writes them, such as MicrosoftWindows. ATT&CK ids are supporting detail.
  • Sides follow MSDL's and C2SIM's force sides.
  • Personas meet the needs the GHOSTS team set out for the Cyber DEM: an account for each service, a pool form, where a persona came from, and no credentials on the persona.
  • What the standards don't model is Ranger's own: vulnerabilities, injects for people, objectives, visibility, and who said what.

docs.title: The Spec
docs.text:
The spec is the C# library Chronicle, in src/chronicle. Apps in other languages use its JSON Schemas, which are generated from it so the two can't drift:

File What schema/chronicle-record.v0.schema.json A whole record schema/chronicle-entry.v0.schema.json One entry, as apps publish it samples/harbor-ttx.chronicle.json A worked example: a fictional tabletop exercise through all four stages

docs.title: The API
docs.text:
The Chronicle API stores Chronicles and carries their entries. Locally it runs in Aspire as chronicle-api at http://localhost:5285, with Swagger at /swagger, and loads the sample exercise. See Local Development.

Resource Routes Chronicles GET /api/chronicles, POST /api/chronicles, GET /api/chronicles/{id}, GET /api/chronicles/{id}/findings, POST /api/chronicles/validate Entries GET /api/chronicles/{id}/entries, GET /api/chronicles/{id}/entries/{sequence}, POST /api/chronicles/{id}/entries Subscription GET /api/chronicles/{id}/entries/stream: server-sent events, the history first and then each new entry Live GET /api/chronicles/{id}/live: a WebSocket with the subscribers, activity, new entries and agents' words as they're written Activity POST /api/chronicles/{id}/activity (with an entry, it's notable and stored), GET /api/chronicles/{id}/activity Subscribers GET /api/chronicles/{id}/subscribers, PUT/DELETE /api/chronicles/{id}/subscribers/{subscriberId}, POST …/{subscriberId}/run Context GET /api/chronicles/{id}/context: a view as text a model can read, with what it withholds Schema GET /api/schema/record, GET /api/schema/entry

Activity is the live feed, kept in memory (the last 1,000 per Chronicle). Only notable activity, the kind that carries an entry, becomes part of the record. Subscribers are stored with the Chronicle; one registered with an agent can be run, and its output is published back. The Chronicle UI shows all of it, live, on each event's Subscribers page.

Every read is an audience's view: ?audience=participant (the default), excon or designer, and ?viewers= for the personas or pools a simulated user speaks for. Entry reads and subscriptions also filter by parts, kinds and after.

No authentication yet

The API takes the audience a caller asks for on trust. Don't expose it beyond a development range.

docs.title: Why It Matters for AI
docs.text:
A language model doesn't know your exercise. Give it the Chronicle and it stops guessing. Because the record is structured, each AI gets exactly the parts its job needs, not a pile of documents. That matters most on a closed range, where a smaller local model has room for less context.

AI at work Reads from the Chronicle Never sees Scenario agent (Scenario Builder) The designer's sources and the scenario so far Nothing held back: it works for the designer Simulated users (GHOSTS) Their persona and organization, their platforms, events as they happen The ground truth and the plan Content generation The world, the information environment, the planned events Designer-only notes Exercise control assistant (next) The intent, the ground truth, the escalation steps, what has happened Nothing held back: it works for exercise control After-action analyst (next) Everything: intent, what was built, every inject, decision and action Nothing held back: it reports to designers

docs.title: Where It Stands
docs.text:
• Today: Scenario Builder writes the world and intent. GraySpace builds a range from them. GHOSTS runs the simulated users. The Chronicle spec is drafted, and the Chronicle API stores Chronicles, takes entries and streams them to subscribers.
  • Next: agreeing the spec's open decisions, authentication for the API, and every app publishing what it built, did and saw: Scenario Builder first, then GHOSTS subscribing.

docs.title: Local Development
docs.text: The repository includes a devcontainer and an Aspire AppHost that starts every service together.

docs.title: Start Everything
docs.text:
1. Open the repository in its devcontainer.
  2. Install node_modules in src/chronicle/ui and the Scenario Builder's in src/scenario-builder/ui and src/scenario-builder/agent. On the devcontainer's mount, npm install can fail with ENOTDIR; the Scenario Builder README shows the workaround.
  3. Press F5 in VS Code ("Aspire: RangerAI (all services)"), or run aspire run from the repository root.
  4. Watch logs and status in the Aspire dashboard at http://localhost:15180.
Service URL What chronicle-api http://localhost:5285 Chronicle API: publish and subscribe to Chronicles (Swagger at /swagger) chronicle-ui http://localhost:4320 Chronicle Angular UI: lists events and opens each one (proxies /api to :5285) scenario-builder-api http://localhost:5280 Scenario Builder .NET API scenario-builder-ui http://localhost:4310 Scenario Builder Angular UI (proxies /api to :5280)

Ollama, LiteLLM and the stand-in fake model server (:5299) are started separately. See Scenario Builder › Models.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
dotnet test src/RangerAI.slnx

The Chronicle tests also check that the generated JSON Schemas and the sample in src/chronicle are current. After changing a Chronicle type, regenerate them with CHRONICLE_UPDATE=1 dotnet test src/chronicle/Chronicle.Tests and review the diff.

docs.title: Adding a Project
docs.text: New parts are added to the AppHost in src/apphost. See its README for .NET, Node and Python projects.

docs.title: These Docs
docs.text: The site is built with Material for MkDocs. Run mkdocs serve from the repository root to preview it at http://localhost:8000. See contributing.md.

docs.title: Range Automation
docs.text:
Next

Range Automation comes after Scenario Builder and Chronicle. This page describes where it's headed. Nothing here is built yet.

Range Automation takes a scenario from the Chronicle and makes it happen on a range. It will:

  • Build the environment from the scenario's topology, through each range's own API: GraySpace, Crucible and others.
  • Run the people by driving GHOSTS NPCs with personas, organizations and timelines taken from the Chronicle.
  • Deliver injects on schedule, or in response to what participants do.
  • Help exercise control steer play, with an assistant that sees the intent, the ground truth and what has happened so far.
  • Write it all back to the Chronicle (what was built, what each NPC did, every inject), so the after-action review compares the plan with reality.

docs.title: What Exists Today
docs.text: Scenario Builder's Topology page can already deploy a scenario's range to a GraySpace. See Scenario Builder. Updraft is a read-only preview and Crucible is a stub, for now. Range Automation will build on that work.

docs.title: Scenario Builder
docs.text:
Experimental

Scenario Builder is under active development, and its screens and data change often. The design documents are in src/scenario-builder/docs.

Scenario Builder walks someone who isn't an engineer through the questions that lead to a very good scenario. It keeps every decision and artifact consistent, and it works on a local model.

It's a structured workspace with an AI agent in a side panel. Nobody starts at an empty prompt: the Questions page is the spine, and the agent asks one question at a time, with a recommended answer first.

docs.title: Key Ideas
docs.text:
Idea Meaning Scenario type A kind of scenario, such as a Crucible tabletop or a small unit team exercise. It defines the stages, questions, gates, checks and outputs. Admins manage scenario types in Admin › Scenario Types, and a model can draft one from a few sentences. Stage A group of questions, answered before the next group opens. Gate What must be true before the next stage opens, for example "the owner approved the executive summary". Ledger The record of every question: open, answered or delegated, with who decided each answer, when and why. Stated vs. proposed A stated answer came from a person. A proposed answer came from the agent, after "you decide" or by inference, and is shown as such. Proposal A suggested change to a stated answer, shown as a card. The scenario's owner applies or discards it.

The model chooses the wording and the order of the questions, but nothing counts as answered until a tool records it. The agent can edit delegated items and wording directly, and every edit is logged and can be reverted. Changing anything a person stated takes a proposal.

docs.title: The Workspace
docs.text:
Each scenario has these pages:

  • Context: source documents and background for the scenario.
  • Questions: every question by stage, with the agent panel alongside.
  • Summary: the scenario as it stands.
  • Topology (for scenario types with a range): the network and hosts, and where to deploy them.
  • Decision log: every answer and edit, with who made it and why.
  • Finish: the scenario JSON, documents rendered from templates, and "send to" buttons.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
A scenario is one document, the full scenario JSON, described by schema/exercise-document.v0.schema.json. Other tools pull it from GET /api/scenarios/{id}. Everything else is rendered from it:

  • Documents people read (read-ins, facilitator packs, designer reviews) come from template libraries: HTML or Markdown with Liquid placeholders, managed in Admin › Libraries. Each template declares its audience, and the builder removes everything that audience may not see before filling it in.
  • Send to buttons for Blueprint, CITE, Gallery, Player, Steamfitter and GHOSTS are in place but answer "not connected yet".

Documents can be made at any stage. While a scenario has open findings, each document carries a draft banner.

docs.title: Topology and Deploy
docs.text: A scenario type with a range has a Topology page. Deploy to GraySpace connects to a GraySpace, shows what it offers (its base, attachment points, images and roles), and builds and deploys the scenario's sites, segments and hosts. An Updraft screen shows a read-only preview of what Updraft offers, but isn't connected yet. Crucible is a stub. This is where Range Automation begins.

docs.title: Models
docs.text:
The API is the only path to a model, so keys stay on the server. Models are configured under ModelServers in the API's appsettings.json:

  • gemma4:26b on Ollama: the target local model. Give it at least a 32k context, or it silently drops the start of the conversation.
  • A frontier model through LiteLLM, such as Sonnet on Bedrock.
  • fake: a rule-driven stand-in for plumbing checks.

Whether gemma-4-26b can guide a designer as well as a frontier model is measured, not assumed: an evaluation runs a scripted designer against both models and scores each run on structural checks.

docs.title: Run It
docs.text: See Local Development, or the Scenario Builder README for running the API, UI and tests by hand.
